title: Where they fell short
hook: the Stoics lived with slavery and empire, and admiring them doesn't mean agreeing with everything

segments.voice: Yesterday: slave and emperor, Epictetus and Marcus. Your line was the same school. What part were you handed, and what's yours to play? Day two hundred ninety-seven.

Everybody has had a hero who turned out to be a person. A coach, a grandparent, a musician whose songs got you through a hard year, and then one day you learn something about them that doesn't fit. What do you do with that? Throw them out entirely? Pretend you didn't hear it? There's a third way, and this path has been quoting the Stoics for most of a year, so we owe it to them, and to you, to try it here. Today: where they fell short.
screen: `A HERO WHO TURNED OUT TO BE A PERSON.` → `THROW OUT, OR PRETEND?` → `A THIRD WAY.`

segments.voice: Start with slavery. The Stoics said all humans share the same reason, that we're citizens of one world, that a slave's mind is as free as an emperor's. And they lived in a society built on slavery, and never, as far as we know, called for ending it. Seneca wrote a famous letter telling his friend to treat enslaved people as human beings: eat with them, speak kindly, remember that fortune could swap your places. That's real, and it was more than many Romans said. But Seneca himself owned many people, and the letter asks for kinder masters, not for no masters. Then wealth and power. Seneca was enormously rich while writing about the simple life, and he served as adviser to Nero. When Nero had his own mother killed, the historian Tacitus reports that Seneca was believed to have written the letter explaining it to the Senate. Marcus Aurelius spent much of his reign at war, and Christians were put to death in parts of the empire while he ruled; historians still debate how much he knew or directed. So what do we do? The Stoics themselves give us the tool. Epictetus said no one is a finished sage; everyone is making progress, or not. They never claimed to be perfect. Admiring them honestly means keeping the teaching that holds, the dichotomy of control, the circles, the citadel, and naming plainly where they didn't live up to their own best ideas. Which raises the uncomfortable question. What will people three hundred years from now say we couldn't see?
screen: `ONE REASON, AND A SLAVE SOCIETY.` · `KINDER MASTERS, NOT NO MASTERS.` · `WEALTH, NERO, WAR.` · `KEEP WHAT HOLDS, NAME WHAT DOESN'T.` · then, large: `HONEST ADMIRATION.`

segments.voice: Let yourself wonder about our own time. What do almost all of us accept, the way Romans accepted slavery, that people later might find hard to believe? You don't need a perfect answer. Just let one candidate come up. Hold it without defending yourself or beating yourself up. Only notice. The bell holds the time.
Where they fell short. The Stoics taught one shared humanity while living with slavery, wealth and empire: admire them honestly, not blindly. Today's word.
Your line: honest admiration. Today, name one blind spot of our time to yourself, and one thing you admire in someone that still holds despite their flaws. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Many modern readers of the Stoics keep their practical teachings while openly acknowledging the Stoics' acceptance of slavery and their entanglement with wealth and imperial power.

fork.reveal: the Stoics called themselves people making progress; we can keep the teaching and say plainly where they fell short.
